paragraphs.text: On a Saturday morning in a mid-sized town, a car park that sits empty for most of the week is transformed. By eight o'clock, rows of striped awnings have gone up, the smell of fresh bread and frying onions drifts between the stalls, and a steady crowd is moving slowly from one table to the next. Scenes like this were becoming rare a generation ago, when many people assumed that the outdoor market was a relic that would quietly disappear. Instead, in towns and cities across many countries, street markets are enjoying a remarkable second life, and they are attracting customers who would once never have thought of shopping outdoors.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The decline had several causes. As car ownership spread in the second half of the twentieth century, families began doing one large weekly shop at supermarkets, where everything they needed could be found under one roof and parking was free. Home refrigerators and freezers meant that fresh food no longer had to be bought every day or two, which removed one of the market's great advantages. Out-of-town shopping centres drew trade away from high streets more generally, and as customer numbers fell, many traders retired without anyone to replace them. In some places the market shrank to a handful of stalls selling cheap household goods, which only reinforced the impression that it belonged to the past.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: So what has changed? Part of the answer lies, perhaps surprisingly, with the internet. When almost anything can be ordered online and delivered the next day, buying in person has become less of a necessity and more of an outing. People increasingly go to a market not simply to collect groceries but to enjoy the atmosphere, try something unfamiliar and talk to the person who grew the vegetables or baked the cake. Growing interest in where food comes from has helped too: many shoppers like being able to ask how a cheese was made or why the tomatoes look different from those in a supermarket. For them, the conversation is part of what they are paying for.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Markets have also become attractive to people starting a business. Renting a shop means signing a lease, fitting out the premises and paying bills long before the first customer walks in, whereas a market pitch can often be hired for a single day. Ayumi Kerrigan began selling home-made dumplings from a folding table four years ago. 'I had no idea whether anyone would want them,' she says. 'The stall let me experiment cheaply. If a filling didn't sell, I simply stopped making it the following week.' Within two years she had a loyal following and enough savings to open a small café. She still keeps her stall, though, partly because it is where new customers first discover her food.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The benefits may extend beyond the stalls themselves. Viktor Szabo, an urban economist, spent a year counting pedestrians in one town centre and interviewing nearby shopkeepers. He found that on market days, cafés and shops within a few streets of the market reported noticeably more visitors than on other days of the week, and several owners said they now timed special offers to coincide with the market. Szabo is careful not to overstate his findings. 'This was one town with a well-established market,' he points out. 'A new market in a struggling area might not have the same effect, and it could even compete with existing shops.' Still, he believes his results challenge the idea that markets simply take trade away from the high street.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes the revival, however. In some cities, markets that once sold inexpensive fruit, vegetables and clothing have been redeveloped as 'food halls' or weekend attractions aimed at visitors, with pitch fees to match. Long-standing traders who relied on small profit margins have found themselves unable to afford a place, and some of their regular customers, often older or on low incomes, complain that there is now little they can buy. Residents living close to busy markets have raised other concerns, such as noise, litter and early-morning deliveries. Critics argue that a market which no longer serves its own neighbourhood has lost something important, however popular it may be.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Graciela Moutinho, who manages a weekly market in a former railway yard, thinks the answer lies in careful planning. Her market reserves around a third of its pitches for stalls selling everyday essentials, and these traders pay a reduced fee, which is partly covered by higher charges for the more fashionable food stands. She also holds a monthly meeting at which residents can raise problems directly with stallholders. 'A good market should feel like it belongs to the people who live nearby,' she says. 'Visitors are welcome, but if we only cater for them, we will end up as just another tourist attraction.' It is a balance that many organisers are still trying to find, but the crowds filling car parks every weekend suggest it is worth the effort.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Back on the Street

A. On a Saturday morning in a mid-sized town, a car park that sits empty for most of the week is transformed. By eight o'clock, rows of striped awnings have gone up, the smell of fresh bread and frying onions drifts between the stalls, and a steady crowd is moving slowly from one table to the next. Scenes like this were becoming rare a generation ago, when many people assumed that the outdoor market was a relic that would quietly disappear. Instead, in towns and cities across many countries, street markets are enjoying a remarkable second life, and they are attracting customers who would once never have thought of shopping outdoors.

B. The decline had several causes. As car ownership spread in the second half of the twentieth century, families began doing one large weekly shop at supermarkets, where everything they needed could be found under one roof and parking was free. Home refrigerators and freezers meant that fresh food no longer had to be bought every day or two, which removed one of the market's great advantages. Out-of-town shopping centres drew trade away from high streets more generally, and as customer numbers fell, many traders retired without anyone to replace them. In some places the market shrank to a handful of stalls selling cheap household goods, which only reinforced the impression that it belonged to the past.

C. So what has changed? Part of the answer lies, perhaps surprisingly, with the internet. When almost anything can be ordered online and delivered the next day, buying in person has become less of a necessity and more of an outing. People increasingly go to a market not simply to collect groceries but to enjoy the atmosphere, try something unfamiliar and talk to the person who grew the vegetables or baked the cake. Growing interest in where food comes from has helped too: many shoppers like being able to ask how a cheese was made or why the tomatoes look different from those in a supermarket. For them, the conversation is part of what they are paying for.

D. Markets have also become attractive to people starting a business. Renting a shop means signing a lease, fitting out the premises and paying bills long before the first customer walks in, whereas a market pitch can often be hired for a single day. Ayumi Kerrigan began selling home-made dumplings from a folding table four years ago. 'I had no idea whether anyone would want them,' she says. 'The stall let me experiment cheaply. If a filling didn't sell, I simply stopped making it the following week.' Within two years she had a loyal following and enough savings to open a small café. She still keeps her stall, though, partly because it is where new customers first discover her food.

E. The benefits may extend beyond the stalls themselves. Viktor Szabo, an urban economist, spent a year counting pedestrians in one town centre and interviewing nearby shopkeepers. He found that on market days, cafés and shops within a few streets of the market reported noticeably more visitors than on other days of the week, and several owners said they now timed special offers to coincide with the market. Szabo is careful not to overstate his findings. 'This was one town with a well-established market,' he points out. 'A new market in a struggling area might not have the same effect, and it could even compete with existing shops.' Still, he believes his results challenge the idea that markets simply take trade away from the high street.

F. Not everyone welcomes the revival, however. In some cities, markets that once sold inexpensive fruit, vegetables and clothing have been redeveloped as 'food halls' or weekend attractions aimed at visitors, with pitch fees to match. Long-standing traders who relied on small profit margins have found themselves unable to afford a place, and some of their regular customers, often older or on low incomes, complain that there is now little they can buy. Residents living close to busy markets have raised other concerns, such as noise, litter and early-morning deliveries. Critics argue that a market which no longer serves its own neighbourhood has lost something important, however popular it may be.

G. Graciela Moutinho, who manages a weekly market in a former railway yard, thinks the answer lies in careful planning. Her market reserves around a third of its pitches for stalls selling everyday essentials, and these traders pay a reduced fee, which is partly covered by higher charges for the more fashionable food stands. She also holds a monthly meeting at which residents can raise problems directly with stallholders. 'A good market should feel like it belongs to the people who live nearby,' she says. 'Visitors are welcome, but if we only cater for them, we will end up as just another tourist attraction.' It is a balance that many organisers are still trying to find, but the crowds filling car parks every weekend suggest it is worth the effort.

questions.evidence: partly because it is where new customers first discover her food

explanation.en: Paragraph D says she keeps the stall partly because new customers discover her food there. Testing which dishes sell was why she started the stall, not why she keeps it now.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сказано, что она сохраняет прилавок отчасти потому, что там её еду открывают для себя новые покупатели. Проверка того, какие блюда хорошо продаются, была причиной, по которой она открыла прилавок, а не тем, почему она держит его сейчас.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що вона тримає прилавок частково тому, що там її їжу відкривають для себе нові покупці. Перевірка того, які страви добре продаються, була причиною, з якої вона відкрила прилавок, а не тим, чому вона тримає його зараз.

questions.prompt: Graciela Moutinho runs her weekly market on land that was once a ______.
questions.evidence: manages a weekly market in a former railway yard

explanation.en: Paragraph G says her market is in a 'former railway yard', which means the land was once a railway yard.
explanation.ru: В абзаце G сказано, что её рынок находится на «former railway yard», то есть раньше на этом месте была железнодорожная сортировочная площадка.
explanation.uk: В абзаці G сказано, що її ринок розташований на «former railway yard», тобто раніше на цьому місці був залізничний сортувальний майданчик.

questions.prompt: Roughly a third of the pitches go to stalls that sell everyday ______, and these traders pay less.
questions.evidence: reserves around a third of its pitches for stalls selling everyday essentials

explanation.en: Paragraph G says about a third of the pitches are kept for stalls selling everyday essentials, and these traders pay a reduced fee.
explanation.ru: В абзаце G сказано, что примерно треть мест отведена под прилавки с товарами повседневного спроса, и эти продавцы платят по сниженной ставке.
explanation.uk: В абзаці G сказано, що приблизно третину місць відведено під прилавки з товарами повсякденного вжитку, і ці продавці платять за зниженою ставкою.

questions.prompt: The lower fees are funded in part by charging more to the trendier ______.
questions.evidence: higher charges for the more fashionable food stands

explanation.en: Paragraph G explains that the reduced fees are partly covered by higher charges for the 'more fashionable food stands'; 'trendier' means the same as 'more fashionable'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце G объясняется, что сниженная плата частично покрывается за счёт более высоких сборов с «more fashionable food stands»; «trendier» означает то же самое, что «more fashionable».
explanation.uk: В абзаці G пояснено, що знижену плату частково покривають вищі збори з «more fashionable food stands»; «trendier» означає те саме, що й «more fashionable».
